name: Uma Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. Could you describe a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and lead an electricity line crew that inspects and repairs the tall transmission towers outside town. I earned a two-year technical diploma and know which old fittings shake loose in the wind. I love seeing a difficult repair finished; the long drives and stiff hands after a climb wear me down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does home look like, and how do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner coordinates a public library, and our grown children have their own lives. My lineworker pay is typical, we have about five months of expenses saved and some other utility crews are nearby. Retirement is in sight but not dated yet; I use AI now and then to tidy inspection notes, checking each tower number against my field card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a shorter tower inspection report is a small improvement, not a reason to empty the trucks. The crew still has to climb, test and replace damaged line fittings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead shifts and my partner's library coordination job feel stable in this picture. We have about five months of expenses saved, and our grown children are independent, so retirement can remain a careful choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the transmission tower inspection rota and check the rigging log before each climb. When I occasionally ask an AI tool to tidy an inspection note, I'll compare the tower number and fault description with my paper card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about money, with the ordinary weariness of a long drive to a tower. I would enjoy a little less typing at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where did a tidied report get a tower wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We checked the last windy repair note before dispatch left the yard. My wind-muffled note turned tower twelve into tower twenty in the AI report; my paper card caught the wrong crossing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your retirement planning change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner we can keep our current retirement discussion schedule. A faster report has not changed either wage or the household bills.

say: **Tower inspections** remain physical work despite a quicker report.
**Tower numbers** need checking against field cards before dispatch acts.
think: Our two **household wages** feel secure in this mild picture.
The **five-month reserve** leaves room to discuss retirement carefully.
do: **Keep** transmission tower inspections and pre-climb rigging checks on every assigned span.
**Check** occasional AI-tidied notes against field cards before dispatch.
feel: **Calm** about income, pleased to lose a little typing.
S0.quote: My wind-muffled note turned tower twelve into tower twenty in the AI report; my paper card caught the wrong crossing.
fieldNote: She uses AI **occasionally** for notes but checks each tower number against field cards.
Two stable incomes and a **five-month reserve** support a calm mild scenario.

steps.text: Keep tower inspections and pre-climb rigging checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can book jobs and draft notices long before robots replace a tower fitting. I want our line crew to check any generated climb plan, and I want library staff included when software changes their hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My linework should last, but my partner does a lot of library bookings and schedules. Those hours could shrink before mine, and five months saved is not a retirement fund for two people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll test the approved AI climb planner against four completed tower jobs and write down any missed access or weather limit. My partner will request the library's staffing plan; if hours fall, we'll postpone the planned home repainting and review our monthly spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household wage, though I can challenge a line plan at work. The slower change gives us time to ask for facts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a generated plan misses a wind limit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop at the access gate and phone control if the plan ignored a wind warning. A power-line tower climb can wait; a bad decision at height cannot be undone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What spending would change if library hours fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd postpone the painter first, because the walls can wait. I would not say my partner has lost a shift until the library actually changes the rota.

say: **AI booking** reaches desks before robots can replace tower fittings.
**Climb plans** need field checks, and library staff deserve notice of changed hours.
think: My partner's **library hours** could shrink before my physical linework does.
Our **five-month reserve** buys time but cannot replace a continuing wage.
do: **Test** approved AI climb plans against four completed tower jobs.
**Postpone** home repainting if the library actually cuts partner hours.
feel: **Anxious** about household hours, with time to ask for evidence.
S1.quote: A power-line tower climb can wait; a bad decision at height cannot be undone.
fieldNote: Her own **tower work** remains relatively safe in this moderate change.
The realistic **partner-hour risk** drives household anxiety and a conditional cut to planned home spending.

steps.text: Test approved AI climb plans against four completed tower jobs
Postpone home repainting if library hours actually fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 can change planning and library schedules quickly, while capable field robots arrive around 2031. We should see the tower crew numbers before anyone claims a safe job is guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be about 63 when robots can do the climbs, and I may still need my wage. My partner's library hours could fall earlier. Five months of savings cannot turn two lost pay packets into an affordable power-line retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask the electricity company for its 2028 planning and 2031 tower staffing figures, and my partner will ask the library for its hours forecast. If the library cuts shifts, we'll cancel the repainting; I'll also compare actual retirement income with our monthly bills before changing my work date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about two possible hour cuts, but I have options and no notice of a loss today. Some other line crews work nearby, and my skill is still useful on difficult towers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grown children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our grown children that we're checking two employers' plans and can pay our bills now. I wouldn't ask them to make up a future gap that has not happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you look at another line employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look for a nearby lead lineworker opening if my company posted tower crew cuts. I would not leave a wage on a rumour, and I would not call an income enquiry a decision to retire.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes plans and library schedules before 2031 field robots arrive.
The electricity company should publish **tower crew figures** before promising every role.
think: At about **63**, I may still need line pay when robots can climb.
Our **five-month savings** cannot cover a long loss of both household wages.
do: **Ask** electricity company for 2028 and 2031 tower staffing figures.
**Compare** retirement income with monthly bills before changing any work date.
**Postpone** home repainting if partner library hours actually fall.
feel: **Anxious** about possible household hour cuts, with options and no current notice.
S2.quote: Five months of savings cannot turn two lost pay packets into an affordable power-line retirement.
fieldNote: She separates **2028 desk exposure** from 2031 physical tower robots.
Her partner's library hours and her own field shifts are **possible losses**, not announced cuts.
The retirement calculation is **information gathering**, with no early-exit action.

steps.text: Ask company for 2028 planning and 2031 tower staffing figures
Compare retirement income with household bills before changing date
Check nearby lead lineworker openings if tower cuts posted
Postpone home repainting if partner library hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2031 changes the schedules first, while field robots reach tower work around 2034. Five years lets the electricity company test the machines and workers set the terms for safe inspection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At about 66 I might be ready to stop climbing if our retirement figures work. If they do not, a paid tower inspection role on the ground could help, but the company has not posted one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll join the union safety committee's meeting on robot trial rules and ask for a paid worker who can stop a machine. I'll also take the company's paid inspection-tool course if it includes hands-on use of robot controls and a real field role, while keeping my current wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible income gap if retirement is not yet affordable. The extra years give us time to test and organise, but they do not create a paid post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What safety test would you demand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the trial team to repeat a stop test in high wind and record who has authority to halt the climb. A tower robot without a human stop control has no place beside a live transmission line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the inspection-tool course worth enrolling in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The course must be on paid time and tied to a posted field role with a wage that covers our bills. I would not enrol in a screen-only briefing and call it a new trade.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes schedules before field robots reach towers around 2034.
**Stop authority** and real wind tests belong in any tower robot trial.
think: At about **66**, retirement might work if our figures are sound.
A paid **ground inspection role** may help if I still need wages, but none is posted.
do: **Join** union safety committee meeting on robot stop rules.
**Take** funded inspection training with robot controls on paid time if a posted field job covers household bills.
feel: **Anxious** about an income gap, with time to test and organise.
S3.quote: A tower robot without a human stop control has no place beside a live transmission line.
fieldNote: Her course is **conditional enrolment**, with company payment, hands-on controls and a paid role.
A union safety meeting supplies **collective action** distinct from merely watching a trial.

steps.text: Join union safety committee meeting on robot stop rules
Take funded inspection training on paid time with controls if posted field job covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2036 changes planning first, and field robots around 2039 reach towers when I would be about 71. The decade should be used to train younger lineworkers and settle who checks each machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope to have left regular climbing before 71 if our finances allow it. My partner's library work might already have changed, so I want a retirement plan built from actual wages, not a date chosen for a speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year my partner and I will review retirement statements and set a minimum monthly income for our household. I'll keep my line safety tickets current and bring the tower maps to a younger crew member before leaving the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the household numbers, but calmer about robots so far away. I would like a handover that leaves the next crew able to work safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach a younger lineworker at a tower?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show a younger lineworker the windward side of an old tower and why the access path matters. A folder of tower maps will not teach a new lineworker what wet steel feels like under a glove.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a real handover of the maps involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the old tower maps and fault notes to a union training meeting, then hand them to a named younger worker. I want that person to practise the route with a crew, not just inherit a folder.

say: **2036 thinking AI** changes plans before field robots reach towers around 2039.
**Younger crews** need physical tower routes and authority to check machines.
think: At about **71**, I hope to be off climbing if the household budget allows.
My partner's **library wages** may change before retirement, so our figures must be real.
do: **Review** retirement statements and set a monthly income target with partner.
**Keep** line safety tickets current while working.
**Hand** tower maps to named younger worker through union training meeting.
feel: **Uneasy** about the household sums, calmer about later robots.
S4.quote: A folder of tower maps will not teach a new lineworker what wet steel feels like under a glove.
fieldNote: She makes a **specific handover** through union training rather than assuming a passive folder is enough.
Her 2039 work status remains **conditional** on household income after any library change.

steps.text: Review retirement statements and set monthly income target with partner
Keep line safety tickets current while working
Hand tower maps to younger worker through union training meeting

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my partner's library hours could change when thinking AI arrives, then field robots could cut my tower shifts around 2031. Published plans from both employers and a paid inspection path, if a real role opens, would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who still walks to a tower after the machine reports a clean repair. A screen can close a tower repair job, but a younger lineworker must know where the ground is soft and the steel is wet. I want that field lesson paid for.

headlineQuote: A screen can close a tower repair job, but a younger lineworker must know where the ground is soft and the steel is wet.
portrait: **Uma**, 58, leads transmission tower repairs with a two-year technical diploma and experience of difficult wind-exposed sites.
She uses **AI occasionally** for notes but verifies tower numbers against field cards.
Her **typical pay**, library-coordinator partner, five-month reserve and some nearby utilities make two wage risks important.
Fast change leaves her **anxious** about household hours; longer timelines allow paid safety training and a careful crew handover.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could reduce library hours before 2031 field robots threaten her tower shifts.
whatWouldHelp: Published **employer plans** and a paid inspection path, if a real role opens, would help the household.
